newsitem.title: PERU: Peru admits security lapse, promises punishment.
newsitem.headline: Peru admits security lapse, promises punishment.

text.p: Peru formally admitted on Wednesday that a security lapse enabled Marxist rebels to seize the Japanese ambassador's home for four months and pledged to punish the 18 police officers, including five generals, held responsible.

Interior Minister Gen. Cesar Saucedo told Congress there was ample evidence the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) was planning to assault either a Japanese, U.S., Spanish or Ecuadorean diplomatic building at the end of 1996.

"It is proven that the national intelligence service (SIN) provided the police in good time evidence of possible terrorist actions to take place in the capital with the aim of releasing comrades in jail," the minister said.

Saucedo, whose predecessor Gen. Juan Briones Davila resigned just three days before the government mounted its April 22 assault to free the hostages, said the police officers would be tried by a military tribunal on charges of negligence and disobedience.

The 19 accused include former head of state security Gen. Guillermo Boggio Cevallos -- one of a clutch of top security officials who were themselves held hostage inside the residence -- and former anti-terrorism police head Gen. Maximo Rivera Diaz.

Those officers, Saucedo said, did not give sufficient priority to the Dec. 17 cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, allowing a band of 14 MRTA rebels to burst in and take more than 500 guests hostage.
Nor did the police coordinate sufficiently with the Japanese embassy's private security staff, Saucedo added.

"It is proved that the (police office in charge) did not give the real level of importance to this event despite it being obvious the highest dignitaries of the country would attend ... Even more so given the orders to take measures to avoid terrorist actions," Saucedo said.
"This erroneous appreciation of the importance of the meeting resulted in deficient and incoherent planning."
Peru's former police chief Ketin Vidal, lauded for his 1992 capture of Shining Path leader Abimael Guzman, also resigned with Briones and has been transferred to Washington.
Congressmen congratulated the government for its strike against the MRTA, when commandos exploded through tunnels and walls to overwhelm the guerrillas while half of them were playing indoor soccer.

But they criticized Saucedo for not explaining how security forces would prevent another similar crisis. And they warned the government against over-confidence in the fight against the MRTA and the larger guerrilla group Shining Path.
"Everything could repeat itself if the root of the problem is not attacked," legislator Henry Pease said.

"The anti-terrorism police should strengthen again its specialized apparatus," added lawmaker Angel Townsend. "We know that unfortunately since 1993, capable people were transferred because it was considered that the fight against terrorism was not so important."

The legislators also expressed fears that the MRTA, which has threatened reprisals, would target political figures. "There are a thousand targets and the government cannot cover them all," said Carlos Chipoco.
As his interior minister did battle in Congress, President Alberto Fujimori was digesting a new poll criticizing him for scoring political points from the bloody end of the crisis.
According to a new survey by local pollster Imasen, 64.5 percent of Peruvians believe the government is taking advantage of the widely praised strike for political motives.

The survey of 400 Lima residents in the days after the April 22 assault also found that 46.8 percent believe Fujimori, who is mulling a third election bid in 2000, ordered the operation due to "concern about his political future."
Only 27.5 percent said his motive was "what was necessary for the country."
